No. 

The story relies almost entirely on exteriority—focusing heavily on observable actions, physical sensations, sparse dialogue, and sensory details of the setting (the fog, the rattling rope, the lever, the passengers' items). There is almost no interiority; the reader is given virtually no direct access to Ilse's inner thoughts, feelings, or memories. Even at the climax of the story, when she receives a phone call from "Jonas," her reaction is described purely through external actions (looking at the screen, hovering her thumb, putting the phone back in her pocket). Because of this extreme restraint and lack of introspection, the story does not portray a broad spectrum of emotions or achieve a balance between action and inner life.
